title: WIHIC | Name the kind of help that helps you

qcReview.basis: Eight English items 9–16 and the five frequency choices match Fraser (2023), Appendix A Table A1. The appendix’s top answer is Almost Always. Source © Fraser 2023, CC BY 4.0. The project retains C and the eight-item complete-response mean (1–5), without thresholds. This version adds original feedback only, for the student who answered.

interpretations.headline: Name the kind of help that helps you
interpretations.summary:
Lee knows the first part of a problem, then gets stuck. Instead of giving the whole answer, the teacher asks where the problem stopped making sense. Lee can point to a line. A short conversation turns a big feeling of being lost into one step they can try.

Your answers describe how often you felt noticed, listened to, or helped by the teacher in this class. Helpful support can be a question, a chance to talk, or a clearer example. Needing a different kind of help is common. Choose one thing that would make it easier to ask or understand the reply.

guidance.text: If asking in front of everyone feels hard, write down one part you already understand and one place you got stuck. Show the teacher when they check in or during a time set aside for questions.
If your questions regularly go unanswered, you can tell a trusted teacher, tutor, or school adult what would help. Bring one example, such as a question or a confusing step.

limitations: © Barry J. Fraser, 2023. Adapted from What Is Happening In this Class? (WIHIC), Appendix A, Table A1, in The Evolution of the Field of Learning Environments Research, Education Sciences, 13(3), 257. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci13030257 (CC BY 4.0, https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). The project presents one part separately, with its own instruction, scoring of complete answers, and student feedback.
The result is the mean of eight answers about one class. The five original answer choices run from Almost Never (1) to Almost Always (5). If an answer is missing, this part has no score.

Using this separate eight-question form with English-reading students ages 12–15 in grades 7–9 is this project’s scope. This item set has no separate validation or group benchmark. Each part of WIHIC stands alone in the report.
report.disclaimer: This report describes your experience in one class. It is for reflection and does not grade you, your classmates, or your teacher.
